organism: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV), a DNA herpesvirus. Primary infection causes varicella (chickenpox); the virus then persists as a latent infection in sensory nerve ganglia and can reactivate later in life as herpes zoster (shingles). VZV survives only briefly outside the body.
clinicalFeaturesSummary: Incubation period is 14-16 days (range 10-21; can extend to 28 or more days after postexposure immune globulin prophylaxis). Adults may have 1-2 days of fever and malaise before the rash; in children the rash is often the first sign. In unvaccinated people, the rash is generalized and pruritic, progressing within 24 hours from macules to papules to vesicles before crusting, starting on the scalp, face, or trunk and spreading to the extremities - typically 250-500 lesions across 2-4 successive crops, with all stages present simultaneously. Disease is generally mild in healthy children; adults have more severe disease and higher complication rates, and immunocompromised children can develop a severe, progressive form. Recovery usually confers lifetime immunity, though reinfection can occur, more often in immunocompromised people. Breakthrough varicella (wild-type infection more than 42 days after vaccination) is typically milder - usually fewer than 50 lesions, often papular rather than vesicular, shorter duration, less fever - though 25%-30% of one-dose breakthrough cases resemble unvaccinated disease in severity.
epidemiologySummary: VZV is a human-only pathogen with no known animal or insect reservoir. It spreads via direct contact with vesicular fluid or inhalation of aerosols from skin lesions - of either varicella or zoster, though exposure to either always causes varicella (not zoster) in a VZV-naive person. In temperate climates it peaks in winter and early spring, though high vaccination coverage has reduced this seasonality. It is highly contagious - secondary attack rates among susceptible household contacts range from 61% to 100% (zoster is only about one-fifth as infectious as varicella) - and is considered communicable from 1-2 days before rash onset until all lesions have crusted.
secularTrendsSummary: Before vaccination, nearly everyone acquired varicella by adulthood, with about 4 million cases per year (roughly the size of the birth cohort) and 90% of cases in children under 15. Since the national vaccination program began in 1995, incidence has declined an average of 97% (comparing 1993-1995 to 2013-2014); hospitalizations and deaths fell 93% and 94% respectively. A second dose was added to the program in 2007, driving a further 85% decline in incidence from 2005-2006 to 2013-2014 in states with continuous reporting. One-dose coverage among children 19-35 months has been 90%-91% since 2007, and 2-dose coverage among adolescents 13-17 has exceeded 85% since 2016.
vaccineDescription: Two live, attenuated VZV vaccines are licensed in the US: VAR (Varivax), a single-antigen varicella vaccine, and MMRV (ProQuad), a combination measles-mumps-rubella-varicella vaccine. Both are derived from the Oka VZV strain, reconstituted with sterile water, given subcutaneously, and contain gelatin and neomycin (but no egg protein) with no adjuvant or preservative. MMRV's varicella component is higher-titer than VAR's.
vaccinationScheduleSummary: Routine schedule is 2 doses: dose 1 at 12-15 months (minimum age 12 months), dose 2 at 4-6 years. Minimum interval between doses is 3 months for ages 12 months through 12 years (though a 4-week interval is still considered valid) and 4 weeks for persons 13 years or older (VAR only at that age - MMRV is not licensed past age 12). As with MMR, separate MMR and VAR vaccines are generally preferred over MMRV for the first dose in children 12-47 months because of a higher febrile-seizure risk with MMRV at that age.
evidenceOfImmunitySummary: Evidence of varicella immunity includes any of: documented age-appropriate vaccination (1 dose for preschool-age children, 2 doses for school-age children, adolescents, and adults); laboratory evidence of immunity (commercial assays can detect disease-induced immunity but often lack the sensitivity to reliably detect vaccine-induced immunity, so a negative result doesn't rule out prior vaccination); laboratory-confirmed disease; birth in the US before 1980 (NOT accepted, on its own, for health care personnel, pregnant women, or immunocompromised persons - who instead must meet one of the other criteria); a health care provider's diagnosis or verification of typical varicella disease history; or a health care provider's diagnosis or verification of a history of herpes zoster, since zoster can only occur after prior VZV infection.
vaccineEfficacySummary: After one dose of VAR, 97% of children age 12 months through 12 years develop detectable antibody, and more than 90% of responders maintain it for at least 6 years. Among adolescents and adults 13 and older, about 78% seroconvert after dose 1 and 99% after dose 2. A meta-analysis found one-dose effectiveness of 82% against any clinical varicella and 98% against severe disease, and two-dose effectiveness of 92% against any clinical varicella. MMRV was licensed based on non-inferiority of immunogenicity to separate MMR and VAR vaccines, not on its own clinical efficacy trial.
contraindicationsSummary: A severe allergic reaction to a vaccine component or a prior dose is a contraindication, as is immunosuppression from leukemia, lymphoma, generalized malignancy, immune deficiency disease, or immunosuppressive therapy (though low-dose, alternate-day, topical, replacement, or aerosolized steroids are NOT a contraindication), a family history of congenital or hereditary immunodeficiency in a first-degree relative (unless the recipient's own immunocompetence is verified), HIV infection (contraindicated for MMRV outright; for VAR alone, contraindicated depending on CD4 status), hematopoietic stem cell transplant within the last 24 months, and pregnancy. Precautions include moderate/severe acute illness, alpha-gal allergy, recent receipt of antibody-containing blood products (wait 3-11 months), recent antiviral drugs, and aspirin/salicylate use (avoid for 6 weeks after vaccination given the Reye syndrome association). Prior history of varicella is NOT itself a contraindication - when a person's history is uncertain, the vaccine should still be given.
vaccineSafetySummary: The most common adverse reactions are local (pain, soreness, erythema, swelling): 19% of children and 24% of adolescents/adults (33% after dose 2). A varicella-like rash at the injection site occurs in about 3% of children and 1% of adolescents/adults after dose 2; a generalized varicella-like rash occurs in 4%-6% of recipients. Fever within 42 days of vaccination is reported by 15% of children and 10% of adolescents/adults, though most is attributed to concurrent illness rather than the vaccine. Because it's a live vaccine, it can establish latent infection and rarely cause zoster later - about 79% less often than after wild-type infection, and usually mild. Transmission of vaccine virus to contacts is rare (only 13 documented cases through 2018) and has only occurred from recipients who themselves developed a rash after vaccination.
vaccineStorageSummary: Follow manufacturer guidance for storage and handling specifics; see CDC's Vaccine Storage and Handling Toolkit for general best practices.
surveillanceSummary: Real-time PCR is the preferred laboratory method - most sensitive and specific, results in hours, and able to distinguish vaccine strain from wild-type virus. Skin lesion samples (an unroofed fresh vesicle, or a crust) are the preferred specimen. Commercial IgM assays are not recommended due to poor sensitivity and specificity. Because commercially available IgG assays are not sensitive enough to reliably detect vaccine-induced antibody, routine post-vaccination immunity testing is not recommended. See CDC's Manual for the Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases for reporting guidance.

supplementalTopics.title: Congenital and Neonatal Varicella
supplementalTopics.summary: Congenital varicella syndrome results from maternal infection in the first 20 weeks of gestation (risk under 2%) and can include limb hypoplasia, skin scarring, localized muscular atrophy, encephalitis, cortical atrophy, chorioretinitis, microcephaly, and low birth weight. This is distinct from neonatal varicella: maternal rash onset from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery can cause overwhelming neonatal infection (fatality up to 30% without antivirals) because the newborn is exposed without the benefit of passive maternal antibody; onset more than 5 days before delivery is usually benign because that antibody has had time to transfer.

supplementalTopics.title: Postexposure Prophylaxis
supplementalTopics.summary: Varicella vaccine, given within 3 days of exposure (possibly up to 5), is 70%-100% effective at preventing or modifying illness in persons 12 months or older who lack evidence of immunity and have no contraindications. For those with a contraindication to the vaccine, Varicella-Zoster Immune Globulin (VariZIG) is recommended instead - specifically for immunocompromised patients without evidence of immunity, neonates whose mothers had varicella signs around delivery, hospitalized preterm infants (born at 28 weeks or later, if the mother lacks evidence of immunity, or born earlier than 28 weeks or weighing 1,000 grams or less regardless of maternal history), and pregnant women without evidence of immunity.

supplementalTopics.title: Vaccination in Pregnancy
supplementalTopics.summary: Pregnant women should not receive varicella-containing vaccine, and nonpregnant vaccinees should avoid pregnancy for 1 month after each dose - though inadvertent vaccination during pregnancy is not a reason to consider ending it. A Merck/CDC pregnancy registry tracking inadvertent exposures from 1995 through March 2012 found no confirmed cases of congenital varicella syndrome and no increased prevalence of other birth defects, though the number of exposures tracked was too small to fully rule out a small residual risk. Postpartum vaccination of women without evidence of immunity should not be delayed for breastfeeding.

keyPoints: Not reliably distinguished from smallpox until the end of the 19th century
The same virus (VZV) causes both varicella on primary infection and, decades later via reactivation, herpes zoster
Licensed in the US in 1995 (VAR) and as part of MMRV in 2005
Since the 1995 vaccination program, US incidence has declined about 97% and hospitalizations/deaths about 93%-94%
Birth in the US before 1980 is accepted evidence of immunity, except for health care personnel, pregnant women, and immunocompromised persons
A vaccinated person can rarely develop zoster from the vaccine strain itself, but at about 79% lower risk than after wild-type infection
Highly contagious: 61%-100% secondary attack rate among susceptible household contacts
